summary: Describes a profile of the Sieve notification extension so notifications can be sent by email. This is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3834.

plainLanguage.summary: This is one way the new-mail ping can reach you: as a short email message sent to another address.

questions: how does sieve avoid mail loops
subtitle: How a Sieve mail filter can ping you by sending a brand-new email, without starting a mail loop.

tldr.problem: The Sieve notification extension lets a mail filter alert someone through a method named by a URI, but it needs a concrete definition for notifying by email.
tldr.mechanism: The mailto method turns a notify action into a new email message built from a mailto URI, and requires an Auto-Submitted: auto-notified header plus loop protections so that notifications do not trigger more notifications.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that also registers a new IANA registry for Auto-Submitted keywords, and it updates RFC 3834.

today: RFC 5436 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 3834 by adding the auto-notified keyword and the registry for Auto-Submitted keywords.

sections.title: What the mailto Method Is
sections.content:
The Sieve notification extension (RFC 5435) is a framework: a Sieve script can ask for a notification, and a URI says which notification mechanism to use. RFC 5436 defines what happens when that URI is a mailto URI (RFC 2368).

The result is a new email message, called the notification message, sent to tell a recipient about a triggering message. The header fields written inside a mailto URI are called URI headers, to tell them apart from the headers of the message itself.
sections.plainLanguage: A mail sorter can send you a small new note whenever a certain kind of letter arrives. This document explains how to write that note properly.

sections.title: Notify Tags and Capability Test
sections.content:
Each tag of the notify action gets a meaning for this method.

  • :from overrides the default sender, meaning the value used in the From header. Implementations MAY also use it as the envelope sender in the SMTP MAIL FROM command, or may prefer a mailbox that receives bounces.
  • :importance has no special meaning here. Implementations MAY use it to set a priority indication on the notification message.
  • :options is not used by the mailto method.
  • :message, if present, becomes the subject of the notification and overrides every other way of choosing the subject. It SHOULD NOT normally be truncated, although cutting an excessively long value may be sensible.

The notify_method_capability test for online may answer yes or no only when the processor knows for certain whether the recipients are online and logged in. Otherwise it answers maybe.
sections.plainLanguage: The notify command has little settings, like who the note is from and what it says on top. Some settings matter for email and one is simply ignored.

sections.title: Composing the Notification Message
sections.content:
The RFC gives a list of guidelines for building the message. The main points:

  • The envelope recipients SHOULD be the addresses in the URI, including URI headers named to or cc. The To: header SHOULD list the URI addresses, including to URI headers.
  • The From: header SHOULD be the :from value if it has email address syntax and passes the implementation's security checks. Otherwise it SHOULD be the envelope to of the triggering message or an address belonging to the notification system. A from URI header MUST be ignored.
  • The Subject: SHOULD come from :message; failing that from a subject URI header; failing that it is retained from the triggering message.
  • If the URI has a body header, that SHOULD be the body. Otherwise the implementation decides between an empty body and an excerpt of the original.
  • References: MAY point to the triggering message. Received: fields from it MAY be kept.
  • Message-ID and Date are generated fresh and MUST NOT be copied from the triggering message. The Date serves as the notification timestamp defined in RFC 5435.

URI headers named auto-submitted or received are considered unsafe and MUST be ignored. Other headers either come from URI headers or have implementation-specific values.
sections.plainLanguage: The new note gets its own date and its own ID, like a fresh envelope. Anything in the address link that tries to fake the robot sticker or the travel stamps is thrown away.

sections.title: Avoiding Mail Loops
sections.content:
Receiving an email causes another email to be sent, so implementations MUST take steps to avoid mail loops. The required Auto-Submitted: field helps with detection.

  • Implementations SHOULD NOT trigger notifications for messages whose Auto-Submitted: has any value other than No.
  • Messages with an empty envelope sender MUST be allowed to trigger notifications. In that case the notification's envelope sender MUST be empty too.
  • Implementations SHOULD use normal SMTP submission and its retry behaviour, but once the notification is submitted they MUST NOT resubmit it, since that risks duplicate notifications and loops.
  • Implementations SHOULD NOT send duplicate notifications to the same address from the same script invocation. Batching within a short time may also help, and configuration options are a good idea.

The envelope sender of the notification SHOULD be the valid :from value, or else the triggering message's envelope to or a notification-system address. A from URI header MUST NOT override it.
sections.plainLanguage: If two robots keep answering each other, letters pile up forever. So the robot never answers a letter from another robot, and it never sends the same note twice.

sections.title: The Auto-Submitted Header
sections.content:
Every notification MUST carry Auto-Submitted: auto-notified (see RFC 3834). It is treated as a trace field like Received. If the Received fields of the triggering message are kept, the Auto-Submitted field MUST sit above them, as a boundary between old and new trace fields.

The field MUST include one or both of these parameters:

  • owner-email: a quoted email address of the owner of the Sieve script, such as owner-email="me@example.com".
  • owner-token: an opaque token that the owner's administrative domain can use to identify the owner, which protects the owner's privacy.

The RFC's example is a list message about a new sweater. The script sends an SMS-gateway notification with the subject From Knitting list: A new sweater, and the result carries the header Auto-Submitted: auto-notified; owner-email="recipient@example.org".
sections.plainLanguage: The robot sticker says who owns the robot, either by name or by a secret code. If the robot misbehaves, the mail office can find the owner.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Sending a notification is comparable to forwarding mail, so care is needed that confidential information does not go into an insecure environment. Implementations MUST protect themselves against mail loops. One suggested mitigation is rate limiting, for example no more than 30 notifications for a user in a 60-minute period, though any limit will produce false positives and false negatives. Administrative mechanisms MUST be available to re-enable notifications disabled after a detected loop, or to stop a very slow loop.

Notification recipients might not own the script, so an address could receive unwanted notifications through a mail-bomb attempt, a typo or a reassigned address. The owner-email or owner-token value lets a domain track down the script owner, and domains that enable this extension MUST be prepared to respond to complaints.

Gateways into other services such as SMS often lose information that is needed to avoid loops and contact the owner. Gateway developers should preserve as much as possible, including trace headers and Auto-Submitted.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could make a robot send lots of notes to a person who does not want them. The sticker lets the mail office find who set the robot up and switch it off.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers the Sieve notification mechanism named mailto, with mechanism URI RFC 2368 and no mechanism-specific options.

Because RFC 3834 defines no registry for Auto-Submitted keywords, this document creates one, using the Specification Required policy. Initial entries are no, auto-generated and auto-replied (all from RFC 3834) and the new auto-notified, which marks a message generated by a Sieve notification system and takes the parameters owner-email and owner-token, at least one of which is required.
sections.plainLanguage: A public list keeps track of the different robot stickers, and this document adds a new one to the list.

items.label: Human-made
items.desc: The message was not automatically generated; same as no Auto-Submitted header.

items.label: Automatic
items.desc: Generated by an automatic process, not a direct response to another message.

items.label: Automatic reply
items.desc: Generated automatically as a direct response to another message.

items.label: Sieve notification
items.desc: Generated by a Sieve notification system; needs owner-email or owner-token.
